prompt: A Microsoft Entra administrative unit named `AU-Sales` contains a security group named `Sales-All`. The individual users who are members of `Sales-All` are not direct members of the administrative unit. You assign Priya the User Administrator role scoped to `AU-Sales`. Priya must reset passwords and update profile properties for the Sales users. Which two statements are true? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. Select TWO.

options.text: Priya can manage user properties for members of `Sales-All` because group membership automatically places those users in the administrative unit scope.
Administrative units remove all default directory browsing permissions outside the administrative unit.
Administrative units can be nested, so create a child administrative unit for the users under `AU-Sales`.
Adding `Sales-All` to `AU-Sales` lets Priya manage properties of the group itself, such as group name or membership.
To let Priya manage the Sales users, add the individual user objects directly to `AU-Sales` or otherwise scope those users into the administrative unit.

assumptions: Azure public cloud. Priya has an administrative unit-scoped role assignment and licensing for administrative unit administrators is available as documented.

sections.correctAnswer: **D. Adding `Sales-All` to `AU-Sales` lets Priya manage properties of the group itself** and **E. To let Priya manage the Sales users, add the individual user objects directly to `AU-Sales` or otherwise scope those users into the administrative unit**. Adding a group to an administrative unit scopes the group object, not its members.
sections.technical:
Administrative units scope Microsoft Entra role permissions to selected directory objects. They can contain users, groups, or devices. Microsoft documents a critical distinction: adding a group to an administrative unit brings the group itself into the management scope, but not the members of the group. A User Administrator scoped to an administrative unit containing a group can manage the group's name and membership. The same scoped admin cannot manage user properties, authentication methods, or reset passwords for individual members of that group unless those user objects are separately added to the administrative unit. Administrative units cannot be nested, so child administrative units are not a solution. Microsoft also notes that administrative units scope management permissions; they do not prevent members or administrators from using default user permissions to browse other users, groups, or resources outside the administrative unit.

The precedence issue is object membership in the administrative unit, not group membership expansion. Microsoft Entra evaluates Priya's scoped role against the object being managed. If the object is the `Sales-All` group, that group is inside `AU-Sales`, so supported group management is in scope. If the object is a user who merely belongs to `Sales-All`, the user object is not inside the administrative unit, so user management tasks such as password reset and profile editing are out of scope. There is no inheritance from group membership to administrative unit membership. Adding users directly, or using supported dynamic administrative unit membership for users, changes the object scope. Administrative units also do not form a hierarchy, so there is no child unit inheritance model to rely on.

wrongOptions.A: Group members are not automatically in scope when the group object is added to an administrative unit. Misconception: group containers are recursively expanded for administrative unit management. Could be correct only if the users themselves are separately added or dynamically scoped into the administrative unit.
wrongOptions.C: Administrative units cannot be nested. Misconception: they work like nested organizational units in classic directories. Could be correct in a different directory system with nested OUs, not Microsoft Entra administrative units.
wrongOptions.B: Administrative units scope management permissions but do not remove all default browsing permissions outside the unit. Misconception: administrative units are a complete visibility boundary. Could be correct only if a separate feature or policy restricted browsing permissions.

sections.plainEnglish:
An administrative unit is like giving Priya responsibility for a specific drawer in the directory. If you put a group card in the drawer, Priya can manage that card. But the people listed on the card do not magically move into the drawer. If Priya needs to reset passwords for people, the people records must be in the administrative unit too.

Priya's permission is attached to a boundary. The boundary contains a group card, not the people cards. She can work on the group card because it is inside the boundary. She cannot work on the people just because their names are written on that group card. To manage the people, put the people themselves into the boundary.
sections.analogy:
A manager can manage files in one cabinet. You place a folder labeled `Sales-All` in the cabinet, but the employee files named inside are still elsewhere.

| Analogy | Azure reality |
|---|---|
| Cabinet | Administrative unit |
| Folder | Group object |
| Names in folder | Group members |
| Employee files | User objects |
| Delegated manager | AU-scoped role assignment |

**Where the analogy breaks down:** Microsoft Entra permissions are evaluated by role assignments and supported operations, and default read permissions may still exist outside the cabinet.

jargon.definition: A Microsoft Entra container used to scope supported role permissions to selected users, groups, or devices.
A role that can manage users, and can be scoped to an administrative unit for supported tasks.
A role assignment limited to a specific scope rather than the whole tenant.
A group type commonly used for access control and membership management.
The directory object representing a group itself.
A separate object included in a group, such as a user or device.

sections.watchOut:
- Adding a group to an administrative unit does not add the group's members.
- Administrative units cannot be nested.
- Administrative units scope management, not every form of directory visibility.
- To manage user passwords or properties, the user objects must be in scope.
- Do not confuse group nesting or group membership with administrative unit membership.
- A scoped User Administrator can manage supported user tasks only for users in scope.
- Adding groups dynamically to administrative units is not the same as dynamically adding group members.
- Administrative units are not a substitute for Azure RBAC scope over subscriptions or resource groups.
- Default directory read behavior can still allow browsing unless separate restrictions apply.

productionTip.official: Microsoft documents that administrative units can contain users, groups, or devices; adding a group scopes the group object but not its members; and administrative units cannot be nested. Microsoft documents exactly what an administrative unit-scoped User Administrator can and cannot do when the administrative unit contains a group: manage the group's name and membership, but not user properties, authentication methods, or passwords for the group's members unless those users are separately added.
productionTip.recommendation: Design administrative units around the actual objects admins must manage. If regional help desk staff reset passwords, put the user objects in scope and test with a pilot account before broad rollout. Recommendation: build administrative units from the objects administrators actually support, then test a sample password reset and profile edit using a non-global pilot account. For least privilege, assign Priya only the role and administrative unit scope needed for Sales support, not tenant-wide User Administrator.

sections.memoryTrick: AU contains the object you add, not everything the object points to. This is especially important for groups because members do not come along automatically.
sections.examTip: Clue words are **AU contains a group**, **members are not direct members**, and **reset passwords for users**. Choose answers that distinguish group object scope from user object scope. A harder version may ask about dynamic administrative unit membership or Microsoft 365 admin center support. The trap is treating the group as a container whose members inherit administrative unit scope. Rule it out by asking, 'Which object is Priya trying to manage?' A harder version may combine this with dynamic administrative units or ask whether the same scope limits Intune device management, which Microsoft documents separately.
